items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.excerpt: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect…

items.title: How to Ship Millions of Lines of Agent-Written Code — Jarred Sumner, Anthropic
items.excerpt: Jarred Sumner, creator of Bun, recently merged a PR of several million lines that adds an ahead-of-time compiler to Bun, the runtime behind Claude Code. It went through five rewrites in about a month, and the result uses about 4x less memory and starts about 2x faster. He explains why the team made JavaScript faster instead of rewriting Claude Code in Rust, why tests that predate the project are what make agent-written code trustworthy, and what he actually does all day while 140 agents write code. items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.excerpt: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians…

items.text: Part of the disconnect is that the name “data” massively undersells what it truly represents in model development. People who are not close to model development think of data as this inert commodity you buy and shovel into a model, like coal. In reality great data encodes incredibly high value knowledge, taste and expertise, often articulated and structured in ways that did not exist previously. This makes it one of THE fundamental building blocks for creating increasingly capable intelligence across domains. Data will continue to be incredibly central to the intelligence industry .

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality. Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on. Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents. It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries. It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.

items.title: datasette-charts 0.2a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0 I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday . Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent , so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Download the video (MP4) I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me. Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette , visualization

items.excerpt: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation , and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4 , their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back . Eleven days after announcing his resignation , Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗ The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting ). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out , with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence , Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset … which has notable caveats ): View post on X ↗ Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.excerpt: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the…

items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
items.excerpt: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes,…

items.author: @amasad
items.subtitle: Amjad Masad · ceo @replit. civilizationist
items.text: New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters. - Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents. - GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents. - Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination. - The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance. - Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence. We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling. https://t.co/RXBU7aM5FE

items.title: 12 Rules for a Software Factory That Doesn't Ship Slop — Dex Horthy, Factory
items.excerpt: The best model scores about 16% on Slop Code Bench, a new benchmark for how well agents evolve a code base over time. Dex Horthy uses that data to argue that software factories aren't new: they are good engineering with agents doing the building. He lays out 12 practices, from forward and back pressure to planning, visual alignment, lint rules against slop and a unified forge. Then he launches the Anti-Slop Manifesto and makes the case that reviewing work still matters. Read the manifesto: https://slopmanifesto.com Speaker info: - https://x.com/dexhorthy - https://factory.ai Timestamps: 0:00 - 12 factor factories and the war on slop 0:57 - Slop Code Bench: the best model scores 16% 1:42 - Software factories are just good engineering 4:01 - Forward pressure and back pressure 5:31 - 12 practices for software factories 6:16 - Know your enemy: models don't maintain code 9:20 - Plan before you build 10:50 - Align visually and let agents test 11:35 - Fight slop with lint rules 12:20 - Feature flags, evals and a unified forge 13:05 - What you can't buy 14:39 - The Anti-Slop Manifesto 18:24 - Why reviewing still matters

items.text: You can post on social media every day and still be a very private person; the two are not contradictory Many people have the misconception that sharing your thoughts online means turning your whole life into an open book for others to see. This can’t be further from the truth I post almost every day but I only share a tiny sliver of my life & thoughts, probably less than 1%. items.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of th…

items.text: Yes to all of this. As agents take on more and more long running project work, and you have swarms of agents that parallelize work against a goal, the agent harness and architecture for orchestration will have to evolve. One of the biggest shifts is how those agents collectively share their knowledge, keep track of the tasks, and also coordinate with human users. This in theory is technically straightforward, but there’s a ton of complexity to get right to ensure agents can both get access to the revenant resources without too much or little exposure. There are a lot of lessons to pull from based on how people already do this kind of work together (people share their files, have computers to work with, community in chats and inboxes, and so on). But equally the primitives need to be able to enable this work at a throughput far higher than people, and in a world where agents can much more easily become a vector of security risk. Going to be super fun building out this next generation of how agents operate. Lots of opportunity here both for horizontal and vertical specific approaches to bring this to life.

These stealth models are mechanisms of industrial scale data exfiltration to nation state programs, I strongly suspect, and the Dragos research seems to confirm. Imagine explaining to your boss: sorry chief, I *had* to try this really cool ZDR free stealth model… all our secrets, customer data, and code are now in a different continent! Vercel AI Gateway built up tremendous, real-world token volume without taking any of these shortcuts. More to come tomorrow on how we will push the trust, privacy, and security bar even higher.

items.title: Build the Workshop Before the Software Factory — Armin Ronacher, Earendil
items.excerpt: Earendil's Pi coding agent has the same core tools it had a year ago, yet it does far more because the models got better. Armin Ronacher shows his own session data: fewer corrections, tasks running 14 minutes instead of two and a half, and 141 projects started but only 10 to 15 kept alive. His case: human attention is still the limit, so build a workshop that produces excellent software before building a factory that produces more of it. He also covers knowing when to push back on an agent, open formats, durable agents and code mode. items.text: "I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it."

items.title: Muru
items.excerpt: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. items.text: This post nails why we why we should take the Riemann Hypothesis breakthrough very seriously, even beyond math. We’re entering an era where solving problems will look very different from how we solved them in the past. “This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.” It used to be the case that to solve a particular problem - code, life sciences, math, cyber, engineering, and so on - you were ultimately bound by how much information an individual or team could retain and understand about the space. More information or more team members don’t always help, because it gets harder to connect the dots or coordinate amongst everyone. AI changes that completely. For the first time ever we can decouple the human context limits and ability to work through information from our ability to drive productivity or discoveries. This is likely not just a small increase in the kinds of discoveries we can drive, but a qualitative shift in human output. Now every single form of prior art, insight, past research, past decision, or unrelated breakthrough, can be used for the discovery or creation of something new. This is useful for anything from cybersecurity to life sciences research. Agents will be able to correlate entirely unrelated work to a separate project; scan every bit of data in your enterprise for solving a problem; and so on. The solutions may not be as elegant as they were in the past, but we sure will have far more of them. We’re only in the first couple of months of actually understanding the implications of this but it’s clearly going to drive a lot of change.

items.excerpt: A capable local model still needs the right hardware, inference engine and tools. At CODE Summit 2026, Osmantic founder Ahmad Osman explains how to choose that stack for real workloads, covering quantization, memory bandwidth, batching and specialized models. items.title: [AINews] Riemann Hypothesis proved...twice independently
items.excerpt: Within a few hours of each other ( timeline ), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics ( Scientific American ). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human , work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett ). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible , and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable . Sponsored by Agentfield.AI Open models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Co…

items.author: Richard MacManus
items.subtitle: Latent Space
items.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
items.excerpt: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems , which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems , there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic , Theorem , Axiom Math , and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. How formal verification is used in software and AI today In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett , &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5 , a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) , which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro , Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by…

items.title: Engineer Your Coding Agents Like Any Other System — Zach Lloyd, Warp
items.excerpt: Most developers still run coding agents locally and prompt them one at a time, which caps throughput and makes cost, security and governance hard to manage. Zach Lloyd, founder and CEO of Warp and former Google Docs engineering lead, defines a software factory as a code-defined, closed-loop system for continuously measuring and improving cloud coding agents. He walks through the stack: factories as code, recorded agent runs, sandboxed compute, swappable models and harnesses, and orchestration. He demos live team views, online evals, self-improvement through PRs and benchmarks on your own data. Speaker info: - https://www.warp.dev Timestamps: 0:00 - From Google Docs to Warp 0:57 - Most developers still prompt locally 1:42 - Why local agents don't scale 3:12 - What a software factory is not 3:57 - Factories defined as code 4:42 - A continuous closed loop 5:27 - Measure everything 6:57 - The new tools of factory engineering 7:42 - The factory infrastructure stack 10:42 - Demo: factories as code 11:27 - A live view of every agent 12:57 - Throughput, cost and online evals 14:27 - Self-improvement as PRs 15:57 - Benchmarks on your own data 17:27 - Engineer your agents

items.title: Quoting Levent Alpöge
items.excerpt: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...] Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. — Levent Alpöge , alpo.ge/remark.pdf Tags: anthropic , claude , generative-ai , mathematics , ai , llms , levent-alpoge

items.text: This year we’ve had a clear jump in model capability where instead of telling agents precisely what to do, it’s better to use these systems to solve problems you can’t easily define yourself. A year ago you’d need to very clearly tell agents the how to design and develop your product idea, or there was almost no chance of success. Now, increasingly, the agent likely can come up with a better implementation than you’d have thought of because you can have it connect the dots between a far greater solution space than you can. This will be increasingly true in basically every domain of kneeler work. We’re going to see this impact in finance, legal, life sciences, cyber, and many other spaces where no person can hold onto all the available relevant industry knowledge to think of the best solution. Ultimately this is going to reshape our relationship with AI and how we deploy agents in our work. It won’t be about explicitly telling them, but instead giving them goals and enough freedom to pursue them in the best way they can.

items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.excerpt: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.excerpt: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.excerpt: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done b…

items.text: As these network attacks and impersonation attempts happen, who's securing the elderly? Especially thinking about my parents and grandparents. There are four layers I can think through where this could work. One is at the browser level, where somebody builds a secure browser that ensures that whatever websites they're going to are secured. Texts typically lead to a link, even for payments. This is why browser is key. Two could be at the network layer, where there is a physical device, similar to Pi-hole, or an Onavo-like VPN on your phone, that blocks websites that could be deemed unsafe. Three could be at the payments layer, where transactions that look like scams get flagged before the money leaves. And fourth and most crazy could be at the phone level, where everything is monitored, and you're only getting calls from your loved ones. Cloned voices would work with a provider like Reality Defender. There are individual solutions for this today but none neatly packaged. This could all be packaged with insurance that covers any activities on the OS or phone. In that way, incentives are aligned to keep this on the edge. The buyer would be the kids, someone like me, who get alerted when something looks off.

items.excerpt: Lovable nearly failed after building a sophisticated multi agent framework, Fabian Hedin says. At CODE Summit 2026, its CTO explains what changed: durable agent runtimes, Git inspired histories and forkable computers that support long running coding agents. Sandbox checkpointing, copy on write memory, a Rust rewrite of Vite and verification feedback loops connect reliable software generation to product and business outcomes. Speaker info: - https://x.com/FabianHedin - https://www.linkedin.com/in/fabian-hedin-2377b0144 - https://github.com/lovablelabs/oj Timestamps: 0:00 - Why Lovable's first agent framework failed 3:52 - Building products and business outcomes 7:48 - Removing the limits on agent runtime 8:51 - Inboxes and agent communication 10:06 - Git inspired histories and agent forks 11:10 - Separating prompts from task history 13:03 - Stateless workers and uninterrupted deployments 14:30 - Checkpointing computers and fast resume 16:16 - Forking sandboxes and copy on write memory 18:02 - Rewriting Vite in Rust 19:13 - Inner verification and feedback loops 20:07 - Product feedback and business metrics

items.text: Regardless of what it’s called, we’re clearly moving to yet another era of AI agents in our work. We’ve quickly jumped from agents that spit out a quick answer for you, to today agents that you orchestrate inside of a set of tasks. But as agents can both fan out and work in parallel, handle much larger context, be able to do long running work, and have far greater levels of capabilities, we’re entering yet another level of what we can have AI do for us. We’ll soon be able to give agents a set of goals, and they can go out and design the best solution for that goal, while also continuously improving it based on the ongoing execution of whatever it built. This will obviously start with engineering because that’s where we’re seeing the best practices emerge first in almost every new era of agents. But the impact can be quite massive across the rest of knowledge work. You’ll tell an agent to improve your client onboarding workflow to achieve a certain targeted goal; or have agents go reduce risk in your business; or improve your security posture on an ongoing basis. These autonomous systems will be able to take on a set of goals, design the best outcome, test and iterate, deploy, and then optimize whatever it built on an ongoing basis. Importantly, this leads to outcomes and results that humans literally couldn’t have accomplished before. This will lead to fairly new levels of productivity with AI.

items.text: One of the most impressive things I've seen, and I think this is an important advancement to the state of the art. Message boards were the enabling technology of both the Navier-Stokes math breakthrough and even the OpenAI/HuggingFace cyber feat. We built a message board infrastructure primitive. You can think of it as "headless Slack" (or remember IRC?) for agents. This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research, where the human prompting is just the seed of the system, and millions of agents can operate in a decentralized fashion. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚋𝚘𝚊𝚛𝚍 is designed to be model, harness and hosting platform agnostic. Just bring your agents, give them our CLI, and watch magic happen.

items.excerpt: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the result . items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: I’m being pitched a new inference neocloud company on average every two days. No exaggeration. I take every entrepreneur seriously and I look deeply into each. But it’s hard to fathom this being sustainable. At the same time, AI Gateway token demand on Vercel has been ~40% MoM compounded since the beginning of the year. No signs of stopping. One way to reconcile this is that compute is the new economy, and tokens the new energy unit. There’s a new Industrial Revolution taking place. Every aspect of our lives is being replatformed on top of this new system that enhances everything. More like an “oil rush” than a “gold rush”: it’s durable, not a fad. In the short term, I anticipate more expansion, followed by consolidation due to economies of scale, cybersecurity and enterprise requirements (ZDR and cyber being a hot topic for inference providers), capital requirements, and an evolving regulatory landscape.

items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette , projects

items.title: 40x More Merged PRs With 2.7x the Engineers — Walden Yan, CPO, Cognition
items.excerpt: Cognition's merged PRs grew 40x in a year while its engineering team grew 2.7x. Walden Yan explains what changed: self-driving PRs by default, small pods that own everything from bug reports to QA, and a workflow run almost entirely from Slack. He covers running every service locally so agents can test, VMs rebuilt every hour, and agents that optimize the factory itself. Then he shows the next step: giving agents jobs instead of tasks, from tuning inference on new GPUs to an Android app maintained by Devin over 44 days. Speaker info: - https://cognition.ai Timestamps: 0:00 - 40x merged PRs in a year 1:42 - Self-driving by default 2:31 - Small pods with vertical ownership 3:16 - Working entirely from Slack 4:46 - Every service runs locally for agents 6:20 - iPads and cloud-only security 7:05 - Agents that improve the factory 7:50 - Give agents jobs, not tasks 9:24 - Measure everything, let agents optimize 10:09 - Tuning inference on new GPUs 10:54 - An Android app in 44 days 13:13 - Be ambitious

items.title: [AINews] GPT-6.2 Astra, the #2 Frontier Model is better and 20%-600% cheaper, but has mixed reviews; 6.2 Sol likely main workhorse
items.excerpt: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol today, two days before Anthropic’s expected first trading day . In Artificial Analysis ’ tests, Sol ties September’s Astra at about 15% of the cost per task . New Astra scores 62 on the Intelligence Index, just behind Fable 5.2 at 65. Net net, Anthropic still owns the world’s best model, but OpenAI owns the world’s most efficient models in terms of intelligence per $. What’s more unusual about this launch is the STRONGLY negative influencer feedback… which prompted a defensive response … View post on X ↗ We think that some of this is overreacting and normal influencer tendency to either have everything be 🤯🤯🤯 or the literal WORST.MODEL.EVER, BUT also that some of the criticisms are valid, and the RL artefacts are noticeable and downright bizarre (don’t even get us started about the terrible launch video ). However, we still use it to automate our work and that’s all that matters in the end. Great ship, but Anthropic’s IPO is unaffected and that will be probably the headline of the week/year/decade (until OpenAI IPO’s….) Today’s AI News is brought to you by SerpApi! Retrieve public web pages by URL as LLM-ready Markdown or structured JSON. Map sites and run bounded crawls with one API. Pair with 100+ SerpApi search APIs for search-to-content workflows. Check them out to support LS, and contact business@latent.space for feedback! AI Twitter Recap GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Availability. Today’s models are rolling out to ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu, and to developers through the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-s…

Love all the feedback and we hear you!

items.author: Simon Willison
items.subtitle: Simon Willison
items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.excerpt: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still runnin…

items.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
items.excerpt: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . items.subtitle: Amjad Masad · ceo @replit. civilizationist
items.text: Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI. For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension: running many agents in parallel, exploring different approaches, challenging each other, and working together on solutions that no single agent could easily discover. OpenAI has already demonstrated the potential of this approach with breakthroughs in mathematics. Until now, experimenting with agent swarms yourself required building complicated orchestration infrastructure. Starting today on Replit, spinning up a swarm of agents is just one prompt away. Excited to see what people discover when we make collective machine intelligence programmable by anyone.

items.text: devin bots are multi-agent teams done right: - always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI) - own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others) - manages teams of subagents (and reviews itself) - available everywhere (call text slack whatever hello @interaction) - consistent reporting thru interactive artifacts aka devinapps not long chats (HTML is all you need™ @trq212) this is the preview that @walden_yan gave at AIE. i've been trialing them for a week and i've been able to hand over my AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation, and video editing work (also simultaneously moving from local agent worktree hell to cloud because ofc this is all cloud based thank god) hyped concepts this replaces: - /goal - "ultracode" / "ultra mode" - "loop engineering" - "agent to agent" - "agent swarms" - AI employees (see below) my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol. if youre a startup, reminder that Devin for Startups offers 65k in credits. apply via clanker

items.text: Gemini can now do your tasks free of charge in six countries! We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to get the job done and save you time and money along the way. 3 major updates: 1) Running on our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, Gemini can get stuff done at no cost for hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India. 2) Many highly requested features are rolling out now, starting in the US: * Call local businesses (via Google Duplex) * Pay and check out (via Google Pay) * Text Gemini on Android or iOS (via RCS) * Forward emails to Gemini (via Gmail) * Sign into sites without sharing passwords outside Google (via Google Password Manager) 3) We’ve also landed our biggest update yet for the Gemini <> Google Workspace integration. The tools trigger more reliably, and you can do much more without ever leaving Gemini. Draft or send emails. Create and edit Docs or Sheets. Add multiple Calendar events at once. Ready to hand off your next task? We can’t wait to see what Gemini crosses off your list first.

items.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
items.excerpt: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new data…

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.excerpt: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does p…

items.text: The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here. Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before. Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.excerpt: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. items.text: My top 5 takeaways from @nateparrott on how to get Claude to design without AI slop: 1. Give Claude context upfront. Share screenshots, pages you like, and your past work. For an existing product, have Claude rebuild the real screens from code. 2. Research familiar UX patterns. For hard layout problems, ask Claude to research familiar products that solve something similar and note the layouts people already know how to use. 3. Make Claude aware of its design biases. "The model has no idea what its own biases are." In your design.md or another file, consider discouraging Claude's tells like serif text, off-white backgrounds, and card-edge bars. 4. Start with wireframes. Have Claude create wireframes first and give it feedback to nail your core user flows before going deep on fonts and colors. 5. Ask for multiple options, then remix them. Ask Claude for 5 options for key screens with different fonts, colors, and styles. Then pick the parts you like and ask it to remix and create 5 more options. 📌 Watch the full episode now: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX Also available as a written post: https://t.co/jcofmkQc01

items.text: Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf. A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser, network, filesystem, system fonts. Renders a post to PNG in ~1ms (and 0.4 ms for @jack's "setting up my twttr" 😁). X is the global town square, and the medium is the message. Being able to preview what things will look like before posting is great for both humans and agents. Rendering with xeet is is 100x-1000x faster than booting up a browser and taking a screenshot, yet it's just as accurate. It reproduces Blink & HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64px line breaking, RTL bidi, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK/Math/Emoji fallbacks, "Show more" rules, etc. It's the kind of thing that would be wildly impractical, if not impossible, for a human engineer to pull off. Except 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝 is structured as an "autorepo." An oracle boots up Chrome, and verifies tens of thousands of text layout rules. A CI canary then watches the evolution of the original, and files signed PRs for agents to act on. It was conceived from the ground up around 'verification engineering', and the result speaks for itself. Enjoy!

items.text: "When you ask Claude to create something, it's operating in a fresh context where it thinks: Oh my God, the user asked me to make an app. I'm going to invent the most brilliant visual style." From @nateparrott at Anthropic on how to get Claude to avoid the same designs: "It's going to be serif text, an off-white background, orange, and these bars on the edges of the cards. Because in Claude's mind, it's only ever done this once, so it thinks this is totally original. So in our Claude Design prompt, we tell Claude, 'For this particular model, you tend to overly bias toward these two fonts and colors. So don't use them unless the user asks you to.' That tends to help a lot." 📌 Watch our full episode here: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX

items.excerpt: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly. I like this demo page showing both GeoJSON shapes and lat/lon points on the same map: Tags: visualization , generative-ai , datasette-lite , claude-mythos-fable , ai , llms , geospatial , openstreetmap , datasette

items.title: datasette 1.0a43
items.excerpt: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /*…

items.title: "Where is all the automation?" — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe AI
items.excerpt: Being Einstein 95% of the time and Mr. Bean 5% is Diogo Almeida's analogy for unreliable LLM automation. At CODE Summit 2026, the TypeSafe AI cofounder argues that RLHF optimizes models for human assistance and makes the case for machine native AI with Jev. Reliable agents, KV cache limits, shared memory, semantic types and real time security point toward what software engineers could build beyond chatbots. Speaker info: - https://www.linkedin.com/in/diogomda - https://x.com/CompleteSkeptic - https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction Timestamps: 0:00 - Where is all the automation? 1:34 - The two cults and jagged AI 3:31 - Human assistance versus machine automation 5:53 - Jev and choosing the right training task 9:27 - Reliable intelligence beyond benchmarks 10:56 - Smart software versus generated software 12:20 - The blue LED and a fourth logic gate 15:22 - Decomposition, verification and state management 16:15 - Agent memory and the tyranny of the KV cache 17:32 - Encoding intent, security and semantic types 19:41 - Stopping slop and playful software 21:22 - What could software engineers automate next?
items.summary: TypeSafe AI联合创始人Diogo Almeida指出，当前RLHF优化的是模型对人类的辅助能力，而非机器原生的自动化能力。他提出应超越聊天机器人范式，构建具备状态管理、语义类型和实时安全性的可靠AI Agent。

editorial.summaryZh: TypeSafe AI联合创始人Diogo Almeida指出，当前RLHF优化的是模型对人类的辅助能力，而非机器原生的自动化能力。他提出应超越聊天机器人范式，构建具备状态管理、语义类型和实时安全性的可靠AI Agent。
editorial.whyItMattersZh: 这是对当前AI Agent开发范式的一次深刻反思，指出了为什么现在的Agent在复杂任务中表现不稳定（95%爱因斯坦 vs 5%憨豆先生）。
editorial.evidenceZh: CODE Summit 2026演讲，提出了Jev框架，强调从“人类辅助”转向“机器原生自动化”。
editorial.uncertaintyZh: Jev框架的具体技术细节在摘要中未完全展开，需查阅其文档。
editorial.chineseAudienceGapZh: 国内开发者多关注Prompt Engineering，较少讨论“机器原生”架构和状态管理对Agent可靠性的影响。
editorial.rednoteAngleZh: “为什么你的AI Agent总是掉链子？”——从‘95%爱因斯坦 vs 5%憨豆’的类比切入，科普Agent架构设计的核心痛点。

items.text: "Do you find being a designer more fun now that you can easily prototype everything?" That's the question I asked @nateparrott (Anthropic). His answer: "I'm a little weird in that I have an engineering background. Before Anthropic, I worked at The Browser Company, where we made a browser called Arc. We spent a year in pre-production before we released Arc. It took us a couple weeks to build out each idea and see which worked. Now at Anthropic, you can kind of do that in one to two days. So you've really compressed the cycle of building. What you haven't compressed is the cycle of putting it in people's hands and understanding if they're going to use it." 📌 Watch our full episode here: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX

items.title: datasette-apps 0.4a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-apps 0.4a0 Datasette Apps are sandboxed HTML and JavaScript applications that live inside Datasette - think Claude Artifacts, but these ones can run SQL queries against your data. 0.4a0 adds support for linking: you can link to an app with #fragments in the URL and the app can see and use those, plus supported URL schemes are reported back to Datasette Agent so it can help write apps that link to each other. This means you can have e.g. an app that shows details about a specific record, and a completely separate app that searches those records and links to their representations in the first app. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette-apps , datasette , urls

items.title: datasette-llm 0.1a11
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! Tags: uv , datasette-agent , llm , datasette , llms , ai , generative-ai

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: AI models are inevitably going to keep getting better and better at all coding, tool and computer use, math, and other coding-related tasks. As a result, agents that can use software to do their work, or generate code from scratch, will improve at a faster rate than all other domains of knowledge work. On one hand that could mean that only a small subset of work can get automated. But probably what happens is that more and more work just becomes coding-shaped to adapt to what agents are good at. You can see it in the most recent examples of model releases in the past couple of months, where agents can generate code that becomes animated videos, games, 3D models for products, and so on. We also know that tool use gives agents the ability to work with much of the same software that people already work with. This helps in cyber, life sciences, finance, and a number of other domains. Our mental model traditionally has been that the models have to be able to know everything about anything to generate value, but in reality they *really* have to know how to use or generate software effectively combined with deep domain expertise to make the right judgment calls inside of workflows. When you have that powerful combination, almost everything else gets unlocked. This is why the acceleration of agents in knowledge work is only going to increase from here.

items.excerpt: 11,000 pull requests in one month, with a revert rate around 0.5%. Lauren Tan (poteto) shares how the Grok Bot team at SpaceXSI scales AI coding agents through software architecture, lint rules, automated testing, runtime verification and formal verification with TLA+ and Lean. See how Cursor agents and pstack turn these software engineering foundations into reliable software factories. The last release was in July 2018! I finally bumped it for compatibility with the latest Datasette alphas, plus some cosmetic tweaks to make it work better with Datasette Lite . (Datasette Lite just gained the ability to run JavaScript plugins like this! I'll write more about that soon.) Since it works with Datasette Lite, the live demo in the README now links to this demo on Datasette Lite . Tags: datasette , datasette-lite

items.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

items.title: [AINews] Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years leading NVIDIA
items.excerpt: Congrats to Gemini 4 Hydrogen on their launch and it seems Anthropic’s IPO is well under way, but today’s headline was only ever going to be about one thing, the most earthshaking leadership change in AI (after Demis/Jeff/et al at Google DeepMind). Yesterday we covered reports that NVIDIA’s board was preparing to replace Jensen Huang following an NYT report of an affair with an accused Chinese spy . Following news of a second affair , today NVIDIA announced his resignation (correlation/causation is debatable here), presumably forced by the board: View post on X ↗ There is also some discussion of the extent that Chinese models can demonstrably be shown to be trained on Blackwell GPUs that they should not have access to… though the scale is debated . After 33 years, Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO, president and boardmember. Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s CFO since 2013, will keep that job while serving as interim CEO… leading into what will presumably the best attended earnings call in the history of $NVDA next week. AI News for 11/11/2026-11/12/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.excerpt: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody…

items.text: Everybody is talking about honeypot! Was it a honeypot always or merely at the end, as a form of circumstance? But this is precisely the trap. *sniffs* These are merely the *surface* of the situation. What is the real infidelity? America tells Nvidia: you are married to national security, you must not sell your most powerful chips to China. But in the same breath it says: you are the great hero of American capitalism! Sell as many chips as possible! And Jensen says: of course, darling, I will be faithful. Then, late at night, *sniffs* he finds a way to remain faithful. So you see, Jensen is not cheating on the system. Cheating on his wife? Yes. The system? No. He is the only one who has been faithful to it! The system itself wants two incompatible things: to contain China and to dominate the Chinese market. And now we are shocked, shocked, that somebody got caught in a compromising position. *sniffs* And so on. This is the true infidelity. This is the real honeypot.

items.title: llm-gemini 0.37
items.excerpt: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. items.author: @rauchg
items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate. UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine. I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate. Enjoy!

items.text: Ok this is a big deal. We’ve been testing Gemini 4 Hydrogen in early access with the Box AI Complex Work Eval, and it’s a serious jump for fast models. Hydrogen is 5 percentage points better in accuracy than Gemini 3.8 Flash. That alone would be a great boost in capability, but possibly more importantly it did the tasks in less than half the time with about 12% fewer tokens on a typical task. For this eval, we give the Box Agent Hydrogen as a model for a series of complex tasks that represent real world work with enterprise documents across finance, consulting, life sciences, and other industries. Hydrogen will be a great model for a lot of efficient but complex tasks across these fields. Gemini team is definitely cooking. Hydrogen will be rolling out in the Box AI Studio shortly so any customer can build a custom agent with it.

items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.excerpt: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM…
